questions.question: What is an execution context? Describe its components and lifecycle.
questions.answer:
An execution context is an internal data structure created every time code executes. It stores everything needed to run that code.

Components:
1. Variable Environment: Stores var bindings and function declarations (with hoisting).
2. Lexical Environment: Stores let/const. Has outer reference → parent environment (forms scope chain).
3. this Binding: The value of this in this context.

Lifecycle:
Phase 1 — Creation: Variables/functions are set up (hoisting happens here).
Phase 2 — Execution: Code runs line by line.

Types: Global (1 total), Function (1 per call), Eval.
questions.tip: The two-phase model (creation then execution) is the internal reason hoisting exists. Mentioning this impresses interviewers.

questions.question: What prints? Tests scope chain and closure interaction.
questions.answer:
Output: 3 → 2 → 1

Each function creates its own scope. inner() has its own a=3 — scope chain lookup stops there. outer() has its own a=2. Global has a=1. Variable shadowing in action — each scope's a is completely independent.

questions.question: What is lexical scope vs dynamic scope? Why does JavaScript choosing lexical scope matter?
questions.answer:
Lexical scope: A function's scope chain is determined by where it is written in the source code — fixed at author time. JS uses this.

Dynamic scope: Scope chain determined by the call stack at runtime — depends on who called the function. Languages: Bash, some Lisp dialects.

Why it matters: Lexical scope makes code predictable — you can understand what a function can access just by reading it, without tracing the runtime call chain. This enables closures, module patterns, and reliable variable capture.
questions.tip: The with statement in JS approximated dynamic scope — it was removed in strict mode precisely because it broke lexical scope guarantees.

questions.question: What is an execution context? What are its components?
questions.answer:
An execution context is the internal environment created whenever code runs. It contains:

1. Variable Environment: Stores var declarations and function declarations (hoisted).
2. Lexical Environment: Stores let/const declarations. Has an outer reference pointing to the parent lexical environment (forming the scope chain).
3. this binding: The value of this in this context.

Types of execution contexts: Global (one, always present), Function (created on each function call), Eval (rare).

They're managed by the call stack — the currently running context is at the top.
questions.tip: Drawing the call stack and lexical environment chain on a whiteboard is a must for this answer in an in-person interview.
followUps: What is the difference between lexical environment and variable environment?
How many global execution contexts exist?

questions.question: What is the difference between lexical scope and dynamic scope? Which does JavaScript use?
questions.answer:
Lexical scope (static scope): Variable lookup is determined by where the function is written in the source code. The scope chain is fixed at author time. JavaScript uses this.

Dynamic scope: Variable lookup is determined by the call stack at runtime — variables are resolved based on who called the function, not where it was defined. Languages like Bash and some Lisp dialects use this.

The practical implication: in JS, you can always determine what variables a function will access just by reading the source code — you don't need to know how it will be called.
questions.tip: The with statement in JS was an attempt to approximate dynamic scope — now forbidden in strict mode.
